titleText.es: Curiosidad de la Wikipedia: si eliges cualquier artículo y cliqueas en el primer enlace del artículo que no esté entre paréntesis o en cursiva, y repites el proceso, terminarás en
titleText.en: Wikipedia trivia: if you take any article, click on the first link in the article text not in parentheses or italics, and then repeat, you will eventually end up at "Philosophy".
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive title attribute is preserved exactly, including its truncated ending and trailing space; the official English title attribute is complete. The Spanish raster changes the final left-chat username from MIKE1979 to MIKE1970, a source anomaly preserved here. Vision omitted CALIBRE FIJO, ERROR, and the English article heading USAGE, confused several accents and letters, and emitted decorative browser/page strokes as false text. The clearly legible inherited English headings HISTORY and USAGE are inventoried as exclusions; tiny article-body and browser-interface squiggles are illustration rather than reliably readable writing.

Base, de, and plural datos form the standard technical term for a database.

Aparente agrees with the masculine singular expression CI; this adjective keeps the same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
Unos marks the numerical point decrease as approximate, and puntos names the measured unit.

cards.noteEn: A bujía creates the spark that ignites fuel in a petrol engine.

example.en: The mechanic checked the spark plug.

cards.questionEn: Why does the outage make the same person suddenly seem much less intelligent?
cards.answerEn: He was using Wikipedia as external memory, so losing access removes the knowledge he had appeared to possess.
cards.noteEn: The left chat shows detailed car advice supported by open Wikipedia tabs. When Wikipedia fails, the right chat cannot identify even a spark plug or a car. The caption treats that dependence as an extended-mind joke: a tool outside the brain temporarily functions like part of the person's knowledge. CI is the Spanish abbreviation for intelligence quotient.
In technical contexts, calibre can name a tool or standard used to check a dimension or gap.

example.es: Comprueba el espacio con un calibre.
example.en: Check the gap with a gauge.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Fijo describes something that stays set rather than changing.

example.es: El aparato mantiene un ritmo fijo.
example.en: The device keeps a fixed rhythm.

cards.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: After a form of haber, cambiado presents cambiar as completed. With a car part, it often means replaced.

example.es: He cambiado el filtro del coche.
example.en: I have replaced the car's filter.

cards.noteEn: Bujías is the plural of bujía.

example.en: The engine needs new spark plugs.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the person or thing affected
cards.noteEn: When le or les already marks an affected person or thing before the verb, a can introduce a later phrase that makes that person or thing explicit. Natural English may instead use a possessive form or a word such as ‘on.’

example.es: Le cambié la rueda a la bicicleta.

cards.answerEn: runs; is running (a vehicle or machine)
cards.noteEn: A vehicle or machine that va bien or va mal is running well or badly.

example.es: El coche va bien después de la reparación.
example.en: The car runs well after the repair.

cards.promptEs: verbo + adjetivo usado para describir el modo
cards.questionEn: How can words such as claro, alto, or profundo describe how an action is done without adding -mente?
cards.answerEn: In certain common combinations, put the describing word after the verb and keep it in its masculine singular form.
cards.noteEn: A word that normally describes a noun can sometimes work like an English -ly word and describe the action instead: hablar claro, volar alto, respirar profundo. It does not change for the person doing the action. This use is conventional, so it cannot be applied freely to every adjective.
Raro is normally an adjective meaning “strange.” Spanish sometimes leaves an adjective in its basic masculine singular form to describe how an action happens, much as an English adverb does.

cards.answerEn: may; might (as part of puede que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something may or might be true or happen?
cards.answerEn: Use puede que, then put the following verb in a special possibility form.
cards.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive: it presents the following idea as possible rather than as a plain fact. Puede que stays fixed, while the next verb changes to match its own subject; for example, llega becomes llegue and es becomes sea.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes puede que (“may; might”)
there is; there is to be (subjunctive form)
cards.noteEn: Haya is the special form related to hay, ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ It appears when the existence of something is awaited, wanted, doubted, or otherwise not presented as an established fact.

example.en: I am waiting for there to be space.

cards.noteEn: Separación can mean the measured space between two parts.

example.es: Mide la separación entre las piezas.
example.en: Measure the gap between the parts.

cards.noteEn: Correcta agrees with a feminine singular noun.
Electrodos are conductors through which electric current enters or leaves a material or device.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: to see it; to check it
cards.noteEn: Verlo combines ver with lo, which stands for a masculine thing or an idea already mentioned.

example.en: You can check it with a magnifying glass.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”
usually; tends to (before an action verb)
cards.noteEn: Suele is the singular present form of soler. It is followed by another verb in its unchanged dictionary form to describe a habitual action.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of soler followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Soler adds the idea of a habit. Suelo means “I usually,” while solía means “I used to.” The action after it stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form: suelo caminar, solía caminar.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone usually does something, or used to do it?

cards.promptEs: entre + elemento A + y + elemento B
cards.questionEn: How do you frame two endpoints or sides as a range, pair, or contrast?
cards.answerEn: Place entre before the first endpoint or side and y before the second one.
cards.noteEn: Entre marks the range or pair involved, and y joins its two sides. Each side may be a single word or a longer noun group.

example.es: No veo la diferencia entre el azul oscuro y el negro.
example.en: I do not see the difference between dark blue and black.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a contrast while presenting the following information as a known fact?
cards.answerEn: Use aunque, then the ordinary verb form used for a fact.
cards.noteEn: Aunque means “although” or “even though.” When the speaker treats the information as real or already established, the following verb stays in the ordinary fact form: es, tiene, or ocurrió. A different special form can appear when the point is uncertain or hypothetical.

example.en: Although it is raining, we are going out.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an outcome depends on a person, fact, or choice?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of depender, then de, then the factor or decision that controls the outcome.
cards.noteEn: Depender changes for the subject and time, but de stays before the deciding factor. De combines with el to make del; before a question word it remains separate, as in depende de qué elijas.

example.en: The date depends on the weather.

cards.noteEn: Del combines de + el. After depender, de introduces the factor that determines the result.

example.en: The date depends on the weather.

cards.noteEn: Motor can refer to the engine that powers a vehicle or machine.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: some; a few (before a masculine plural noun)
cards.noteEn: Unos introduces an indefinite masculine plural group or amount. Use unas before a feminine plural noun.
Recarga tells one familiar person to load a page or resource again.

example.es: Recarga la página dentro de un minuto.
example.en: Reload the page in a minute.

cards.answerEn: people; one; you in general (impersonal marker)
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person singular verb, se can leave the people doing the action unspecified.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona singular (persona no especificada)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish describe what people in general, an unspecified person, or ‘you’ generally do?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person singular verb and leave the person unspecified.
cards.noteEn: This impersonal pattern focuses on the action rather than naming who performs it: aquí se trabaja means ‘people work here.’ It is distinct from the reflexive use in which someone acts on themself.

example.es: En esta biblioteca se estudia en silencio.
example.en: People study quietly in this library.

cards.noteEn: Pudo is a completed-past form of poder for one person or thing. In no se pudo plus an action, it says that completing that action was not possible.

example.es: No se pudo abrir el archivo.
example.en: The file could not be opened.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Conectar can describe establishing a technical link between systems.

example.es: No puedo conectar el ordenador con la red.
example.en: I cannot connect the computer to the network.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something connects to a system or service?
cards.answerEn: Use conectar con, followed by that system or service.
cards.noteEn: The form of conectar can change for tense or person; con introduces the other endpoint.

example.es: El programa intenta conectar con el servidor.
example.en: The program tries to connect to the server.

cards.noteEn: After conectar, con can introduce the system or service at the other end of the connection.

example.es: La aplicación conecta con el servidor.
example.en: The application connects to the server.

cards.noteEn: Base combines with de datos to form the common technical term base de datos.

example.es: La base de datos está disponible.

cards.questionEn: What is the standard Spanish term for a database?
cards.noteEn: The plural datos stays plural inside this fixed technical term.

example.es: Guardamos la información en una base de datos.
example.en: We store the information in a database.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what normally happens whenever another event happens?
cards.answerEn: Use cuando, then an ordinary present-time verb form, and state the usual result.
cards.noteEn: Cuando can introduce a repeated event or a general fact. For that settled, recurring meaning, both actions can use ordinary present forms. This differs from a specific future event, where Spanish normally changes the verb after cuando to a subjunctive form—a form used when that future event is still pending.

example.en: When it rains, I carry an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of caerse when an online service, connection, or network goes down
cards.noteEn: With an online service, connection, or network, caerse means to go down or drop. Se stays before the changed form of caer: el servicio se cae for one service and las conexiones se caen for several connections.

example.es: La conexión se cae a menudo.

cards.promptEs: caerse un servicio, una conexión o una red
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an online service, connection, or network goes down?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of caerse with the service, connection, or network that becomes unavailable.
cards.noteEn: Caerse is caer with a matching short word such as se. The verb changes to match the number of things: el servicio se cae for one, but las conexiones se caen for more than one. In this technical use, nothing literally falls.

example.es: La conexión se cae cada noche.

cards.noteEn: Caerse can describe a website, network, or service becoming unavailable.

example.es: Cuando se cae la red, esperamos.
example.en: When the network goes down, we wait.

cards.noteEn: Aparente describes how something seems, which may differ from what it really is.

example.es: Su calma aparente ocultaba los nervios.
example.en: His apparent calm hid his nerves.

cards.noteEn: Caer can describe a number, level, score, or apparent ability decreasing.

example.es: La temperatura cae por la noche.

cards.answerEn: about; approximately (before a masculine plural amount)
cards.noteEn: Before a number, unos can make the quantity approximate. This differs from unos before an ordinary plural noun, where it usually means ‘some’ or ‘a few.’

example.en: We will take about twenty minutes.

cards.questionEn: How do you make a number sound approximate, like ‘about twenty minutes’?
cards.answerEn: Put unos or unas before the number.
cards.noteEn: Use unos before a masculine plural unit and unas before a feminine plural unit: unos veinte minutos, unas veinte personas. Here these words mean ‘about,’ rather than their ordinary ‘some’ meaning before a noun without a number.

cards.answerEn: points in a score or numerical scale
cards.noteEn: Punto can mean a dot, a location, or a point in a score or measured scale. The plural puntos counts units on that scale, whether they are awarded in a game or used to state a measured score.
